name: Rugbrod Danish Rye Bread
headnote: The family card records this as coming from Anders on YouTube and reproduces the URL in its cook's note, so the link is the recorded source rather than a found match. The method is a two-stage overnight build: a loose 50g starter / 350g rye flour / 350g water preferment alongside a separate soak of 250g cracked rye with about 250g water and a handful of flax, then both combined next morning with roughly 100g more rye flour, a cup of AP flour, two spoons of malt syrup, sunflower and pumpkin seeds and a heaping tablespoon of Diamond kosher salt. The dough is deliberately stiff - the note says the consistency should be like dry cement mix - which is what lets an all-rye loaf hold its shape without gluten. Baking is 350F for 1 hr 15 min in the pan to above 205F internal, then 15 minutes out of the pan, and the cooled loaf is bagged for six hours so the crust softens.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS - YouTube page could not be fetched (HTTP 429 rate limit, twice). Digest above is built from the family card's own cook's note, not from the video page.
flags: URL was already present in the card's Source field and cook's note; recorded, not found. Video page itself returned 429 on two fetch attempts so no headnote/comments could be harvested from it - a later pass could retry. Gram weights already throughout this recipe.

name: Rugbrod Rye Bread—Food Geek
headnote: Sune Trudslev (Foodgeek) makes a true Danish rugbrod from 100 percent rye rather than the wheat-and-rye blends sold as rye bread elsewhere. It is a sourdough loaf packed with soaked cracked rye kernels and pumpkin seeds, and that heavy soaker is what produces the dense, moist, thinly sliceable crumb Danes expect for smorrebrod. Because rye has almost no gluten to develop, the loaf is simply mixed, poured into a tin and proofed rather than shaped. He gives two levain options depending on whether you keep a 100 percent hydration wheat starter or a 166 percent hydration rye starter.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS - the recipe page carries no visible ratings or reader comments.
flags: Verified line by line against the family card: presoak 330g cracked rye / 170g pumpkin seeds / 500g water and dough 400g levain / 20g salt / 50g malt syrup / 400g rye flour / 200g water match exactly. Only the levain differs slightly (family wrote 125g starter, 150g rye flour, 350g water; site gives 80/140/260 for a wheat starter and 80/150/250 for a rye starter) - a scaled-up home adaptation, same recipe. Note: the collection already carries a separate row 'Rye Bread -' pointing at foodgeek.io with this same ingredient list, so these two rows are likely duplicates worth merging. Entire recipe is already in grams.

name: Scalloped Potatoes with Leeks and Cream
headnote: Posted by a food.com member writing as Miss V of Snellville, Georgia, this is the classic leek-and-cream potato gratin. The leeks are softened in butter first and their liquid cooked off, so they season the dish rather than water it down, and only the white and pale green parts are used to keep the flavor sweet rather than grassy. Cream infused with whole garlic cloves is ladled between the layers, and white cheddar goes inside while Parmesan finishes the top for browning.
comment_digest: Reviewers agree it is rich but easy, and it comes up repeatedly as a potluck and dinner-party dish. The one practical warning is that cleaning the leeks is the fiddliest part of the job. The family's own cook's note adds two useful pieces: slice the potatoes straight into salt water (4 tsp table salt per quart of lukewarm water) to stop them graying while you work, and a mandoline on the thick setting gives the right slice.
flags: MEDIUM because the phrasing of the family's card ('Can be prepared 6 hours ahead. Cover and refrigerate. Let stand 1 hour at room temperature before baking.') is unmistakable Bon Appetit house style, so the true original is almost certainly a Bon Appetit recipe - and bonappetit/epicurious are both on the hard-blocked list, so it cannot be reached or confirmed. The food.com page is a member repost of what is evidently the same recipe: quantities match the family card line for line (1/4 c butter, leeks, 1 T butter, 2 c whipping cream, 3 garlic cloves, 4 lbs potatoes, 2 c grated white cheddar, Parmesan). Only two differences - the repost says yukon gold where the family says russet, and 1/2 c Parmesan where the family says 1/3 c. Card's own source is 'Jan Symmes Gourmet Club', i.e. the family got it secondhand. A human may prefer to demote this to notfound and hunt the Bon Appetit original instead.

name: Scotch Eggs, Baked
rating: Community Pick, 32 reviews (no star figure shown)
headnote: Jenny Sanders offers the baked rather than deep-fried treatment of the Scottish pub staple, on the argument that you lose nothing in flavor and shed a great deal of grease. The sausage casing is built from scratch out of lean ground pork (or turkey) seasoned with sage, thyme, pepper and a pinch of clove, which is what supplies the banger character without buying bulk sausage. Dipping the peeled hard-boiled egg in water and then flour gives the meat something to grip, so the coat does not slide off in the oven.
comment_digest: Across 32 reviews the dominant note is to under- rather than over-boil the eggs: people who cooked them the full time got rubbery whites and a grey ring, so pull them earlier. Second most common is that the baked version browns pale, and reviewers fix it by spraying the coated eggs with olive oil or finishing under the broiler. Several say to double the batch because they vanish. Successful substitutions reported: bulk sausage in place of the seasoned ground pork, fresh breadcrumbs for dry, and almond meal for a gluten-free coating.
flags: Exact ingredient-for-ingredient match with the family card, including the unusual 1/8 tsp cloves and the 2 cups fine dry breadcrumbs. The family card's headnote ('typically fried... just as good baked and a great deal less greasy') is a paraphrase of this author's own intro. Rejected along the way: https://www.food.com/recipe/scotch-eggs-baked-not-fried-76904 , which is a different recipe entirely (bread-and-milk panade, bacon wrap, nutmeg).

name: Seven Layer Fiesta Dip

name: Shrimp Creole

name: Simmered Smoked Links
headnote: Maxine Cenker's slow-cooker party appetizer: cocktail sausages left to simmer for hours in a three-ingredient glaze of brown sugar, ketchup and prepared horseradish. The horseradish is the whole point - it cuts the sweetness of a cup of brown sugar so the links read as sweet-and-sharp rather than candied, and because it is raw horseradish rather than a hot sauce the heat fades over the long cook into a background warmth. Nothing needs browning first; the sausages are already smoked and cooked, so the four hours on low is purely about the glaze reducing onto them. Taste of Home suggests serving them speared on decorative toothpicks.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS - the page shows a review count but no readable review text was returned.
flags: Exact match to the family card, which already names 'Taste of Home Quick Cooking 2002' as its source: 2 pkgs (16 oz each) miniature smoked sausage links, 1 cup packed brown sugar, 1/2 cup ketchup, 1/4 cup prepared horseradish, low 4 hours. Gram conversions for Robert: 1 cup packed brown sugar = 220 g, 1/2 cup ketchup = 120 g, 1/4 cup prepared horseradish = 60 g, 2 x 16 oz sausage = 907 g.

name: Slow Cooker Rosemary Pork and Mushrooms with Shallots
headnote: A plain slow-cooker braise: pork shoulder cut into half-inch slices, browned first in a skillet, then left in the cooker with shallots, sliced mushrooms, fresh rosemary and a can of diced tomatoes. Browning is the only stovetop step and it is worth doing, since nothing else in the pot will produce color or fond. The half-inch slicing of the shoulder matters too - it gives far more surface for the tomato and rosemary to work on than a whole roast would, and it cooks to shreddable in eight hours on low.
comment_digest: The single loudest note across the reviews is that the dish as written is under-seasoned: reviewers double or even triple the rosemary, and many add garlic powder, a bay leaf, or Worcestershire. Crushed tomatoes in place of diced works, and extra mushrooms are a common and successful addition. Served over rice, egg noodles or mashed potatoes rather than on its own.
flags: MEDIUM on provenance, not on identity. The ingredient list matches the family card exactly, item for item (1 Tbsp oil, 2 lbs boneless pork shoulder in 1/2 inch slices, 1 cup chopped shallots, 2 cups sliced mushrooms, 1 Tbsp fresh rosemary, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp black pepper, one 14 oz can diced tomatoes; low 8 hours or high 4). But the family card ends with 'Crock-Pot(R) Slow Cooker' and 'Recommended Unit Size: 3 - 6 Quarts', which is boilerplate from the Crock-Pot brand's own recipe site - so the text Robert copied almost certainly came from crock-pot.com, not from this food.com member page (posted by BeckyF, who describes it as her mother's). Same recipe, probably a different page. Runner-up if a human wants to hunt the brand original: search crock-pot.com. Also seen: https://recipes.sparkpeople.com/recipe-detail.asp?recipe=1405859 (ED's Rosemary Pork Mushrooms with Shallots), another repost. Gram conversions: 2 lbs pork shoulder = 907 g, 14 oz can diced tomatoes = 397 g.

name: Snickerdoodles
rating: No star rating or review count shown on the page
headnote: Betty Crocker's canonical snickerdoodle. The published version splits the fat between butter and shortening on purpose: shortening keeps the crumb tender and pillowy while butter supplies flavor and edges that crisp. Cream of tartar is what makes a snickerdoodle a snickerdoodle rather than a cinnamon sugar cookie - it gives the tang and, working with the baking soda, the characteristic crackled top. The dough is rolled in cinnamon sugar before baking, not after, so the coating bakes into the surface.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS - the Betty Crocker page carries recipe tips and variations but no reader comment section. The family's own card adds the practical steps the published page leaves loose: chill the dough two hours, shape into walnut-sized balls, space 2 inches apart on an ungreased sheet, and pull at 12 minutes at 375F while still soft.
flags: MEDIUM. The card is attributed to Julie Horsley, a personal source, so this is not provably where she got it - but the dry skeleton is identical to Betty Crocker's and unmistakably descended from it: 1 1/2 c sugar, 2 eggs, 2 3/4 c flour, 2 tsp cream of tartar, 1 tsp baking soda, cinnamon-sugar roll. The differences are exactly what a home cook's copy looks like: 1 cup margarine standing in for Betty Crocker's 1/2 c butter + 1/2 c shortening, salt raised from 1/4 to 1/2 tsp, and 2 Tbsp coating sugar instead of 1/4 cup. Robert may prefer to treat this as 'adapted from' rather than a source link. Gram conversions for the family card: 1 c margarine = 227 g, 1 1/2 c sugar = 300 g, 2 3/4 c all-purpose flour = 344 g, 2 Tbsp sugar = 25 g.

name: Southwestern Black Bean Salad
headnote: Cook's Country rebuilt the standard black bean salad by throwing out the two ingredients that usually flatten it - raw bell pepper and raw onion - and using scallions instead, which stay mellow. The real move is toasting the corn in a hot skillet until it is spotty brown, which gives the kernels a nutty depth raw or thawed corn never has. They also invert the usual dressing ratio, running far more lime juice than oil, with a teaspoon of honey to keep the acid in check; the scallions go into the dressing so the lime tames them. Avocado supplies the richness that the reduced oil gave up.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS returned from the page. The recipe's own sidebar carries the one tip worth keeping: use canned beans packed with salt rather than no-salt 'natural' or 'organic' brands, which taste flat in an uncooked salad - and if you only have unsalted beans, marinate them in the dressing for ten minutes before assembling. Robert's own cook's note (8/25) records making it without beans, where the toasted corn carried the dish, and warns off one substitution: adding Wegmans adobo marinade was a failure, use Sriracha instead if you want the heat.
flags: Exact match to the family card, which already names 'Cooks Country 2009'. Ingredient list matches item for item; the only differences are the can size (family wrote 16-ounce, site says 15-ounce) and Parmesan-free trivia. The family card even preserves the magazine's 'WHY THIS RECIPE WORKS' block verbatim, confirming it was copied from the Cook's Country print/online page. Gram conversions: 1/3 cup lime juice = 80 g, 1/4 cup olive oil = 54 g, 2 cups corn kernels = 300 g, 2 cans black beans drained = about 500 g, 1/4 cup chopped cilantro = 4 g.

name: Spam Cracker Spread
flags: Family card, no source. Searched and checked the one exact-title hit, https://plentysweetlife.wordpress.com/2017/01/31/spam-cracker-spread/ , and rejected it: that one is a layered dip (ground Spam with sour cream and onion, topped with a cream cheese layer and green olives), whereas the family's is a single grated mixture of Spam, Colby, sweet pickles and onion bound with Miracle Whip. Same name, different recipe - not accepted.

name: Spinach and Artichoke in Puff Pastry
headnote: A make-ahead pinwheel appetizer: the familiar spinach-artichoke dip mixture, bound with mayonnaise and Parmesan and seasoned only with onion powder, garlic powder and pepper, is spread thin over sheets of frozen puff pastry, rolled jelly-roll style, firmed in the freezer and then sliced into rounds. Freezing before slicing is the step that makes it work - a soft roll smears when you cut it, a firm one gives clean spirals. The logs keep up to three months frozen, so the whole thing can be built weeks ahead and baked straight from the freezer for a party. The food.com poster, Debbwl, credits the Complete Southern Cookbook as the original.
comment_digest: One review only, and it carries a real warning worth keeping: after about a week in the freezer the rolls wept a greenish oil while thawing, so the baked slices tasted fine but looked unappealing. The practical reading is to freeze just long enough to firm the logs for slicing rather than storing them for weeks, or to slice and bake from a shorter freeze.
flags: Ingredient-for-ingredient match with the family card including the oddly specific 17.3 oz puff pastry package; only the garlic powder differs trivially (family 1 tsp, page 3/4-1 tsp). Note the true original is cited on the page as the Complete Southern Cookbook, so a human may prefer to record that book rather than the food.com repost. Gram conversions: 10 oz frozen chopped spinach = 283 g, 14 oz can artichoke hearts = 397 g, 1/2 cup mayonnaise = 110 g, 1/2 cup grated Parmesan = 50 g, 17.3 oz puff pastry = 490 g.

name: Strawberry Nut Bread
rating: No star rating or review count shown on the page
headnote: Betty Crocker pitches this as the quick bread that beats banana bread at its own game. It is an oil-and-egg batter rather than a creamed one, with a full tablespoon of cinnamon and no leavening but baking soda - the soda works against the acid of the strawberries, which is why the fruit has to go in juice and all rather than being patted dry. Two cups of sugar for two loaves makes it firmly a sweet bread, close to cake, and the nuts are what keep it from reading as one-note.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS - the Betty Crocker page shows no reader comment section. The family's card supplies the technique the published version leaves out: sprinkle the frozen berries with a few spoonfuls of sugar and let them sit while you assemble, blend the oil and eggs into the strawberry mixture rather than the other way around, and stir the wet into the dry only until just moist. Butter and flour two 9x5 pans; 50-60 minutes at 350F.
flags: MEDIUM. The family card carries no source, and this recipe circulates widely in church and community cookbooks, so this cannot be proved to be where Robert's copy came from. But the fingerprint matches Betty Crocker's exactly on every distinctive line: 2 cups sugar, 1 1/4 cups oil, 4 eggs, 3 teaspoons (= 1 tablespoon) cinnamon, 1 teaspoon baking soda as the only leavening, 1 teaspoon salt, frozen strawberries. The two differences are trivial home-baker drift - the card writes 3 cups plus 2 tablespoons flour against Betty Crocker's flat 3 cups, and 1 1/4 cups pecans against 1 cup nuts. Gram conversions: 2 c sugar = 400 g, 1 1/4 c vegetable oil = 273 g, 3 c + 2 Tbsp all-purpose flour = 391 g, 1 Tbsp cinnamon = 8 g, 1 1/4 c chopped pecans = 138 g, 16 oz frozen strawberries = 454 g.

name: Toll House Cookies
rating: No star rating or review count shown
headnote: Yankee Magazine's transcription of Ruth Wakefield's original 1930s Toll House cookie from the inn in Whitman, Massachusetts - the recipe that started the chocolate chip cookie. The step that marks the original, and that modern printings dropped, is dissolving the baking soda in hot water before it goes into the dough: it disperses the leavening evenly and produces a thinner, crisper, better-browned cookie than stirring dry soda into the flour does. Everything else is the familiar skeleton - equal white and light brown sugar, a full pound of butter's worth of fat per 2 1/4 cups of flour, two eggs, 12 ounces of chips and a cup of nuts.
comment_digest: The loudest recurring argument is fat: readers who use all butter complain the cookies spread too thin, and a large contingent goes to all shortening or half butter and half Crisco for a crisper, taller cookie. A second group confirms the hot-water soda trick does exactly what it claims - thinner and crispier with more browning - so treat it as a choice rather than a formality. Chilling the dough is repeatedly urged even though the recipe does not require it. Readers also note the original circulated in several forms, with chopped chocolate rather than chips, shifted sugar ratios, and sometimes oatmeal.
flags: The family card is unmistakably the ORIGINAL Toll House rather than the modern Nestle back-of-bag version, because it keeps the hot-water step that Nestle later dropped. Line for line: 1 c butter or margarine, 3/4 c sugar, 3/4 c light brown sugar, 2 eggs, 2 1/4 c flour, 1 tsp soda, 1 tsp salt, hot water, 1 tsp vanilla, 1 c chopped nuts, one 12 oz package chips. The single discrepancy is the water quantity - the family card says 2 tablespoons where this transcription says 1 teaspoon; older printings of the original vary on exactly this line, so it is period drift, not a different recipe. Robert's cook's note calls it 'Mom's standard' and says they usually make a half recipe. Gram conversions: 1 c butter = 227 g, 3/4 c granulated sugar = 150 g, 3/4 c packed light brown sugar = 165 g, 2 1/4 c all-purpose flour = 281 g, 12 oz chocolate chips = 340 g, 1 c chopped nuts = 113 g.

name: Tomato Feta Cheese Canapes
flags: Family card, no source. The dish sits in the crowded crostini-with-soft-cheese-and-tomato genre, and the nearest published relatives are Ina Garten's Tomato Crostini with Whipped Feta (https://barefootcontessa.com/recipes/tomato-crostini-with-whipped-feta) and various bruschetta-with-creamy-feta posts - but the family's is a distinctly different construction, a cream-cheese base with only 1/4 cup feta folded in plus basil, chives and a tablespoon of low-fat Hellmann's, spread on twice-oiled toasts. Not accepted; the resemblance is generic. Gram conversions: 4 oz cream cheese = 113 g, 1/4 c feta = 38 g, 1 Tbsp mayonnaise = 14 g.

name: Tomato Sauce--Symmes family
flags: Named for the family in its own title, so no published source is expected and none was sought beyond confirming. Worth flagging one genuinely unusual technique the card preserves and explains, in case it matters to the project: baking soda (1/4 to 1/2 tsp) is stirred in during the final ten minutes, a little at a time with tasting between, to neutralize the acid of the tomatoes. Nutmeg in the seasoning is the other period marker. Gram conversions: 2 x 6 oz cans tomato paste = 340 g, a No. 2 1/2 can of tomatoes = about 794 g (the card's own alternative, 3 1/2 cups fresh peeled, is about 790 g), 2 Tbsp olive oil = 27 g, 1/4 c grated Parmesan = 25 g, 1/2 lb meat or meatballs = 227 g.

name: Tortilla Pie
flags: Heavily abbreviated family card with transcription garble ('Png flour tortillas 10, 5 ea stack', 'Last layou only cheese'). A stack of flour tortillas layered with condensed cream of chicken soup, shredded cheddar and canned chopped chilies, baked 350F for half an hour. Searched the genre and found only full chicken-tortilla casseroles, which are a different and much larger dish. Not accepted. Note this row and 'Tortilla Wedges' are near-duplicates of each other - same construction, soup swapped from chicken to mushroom - and a human may want to merge them.

name: Tortilla Wedges
flags: Family card, no source, and a near-duplicate of 'Tortilla Pie' in this same batch: large flour tortillas layered with a can of cream of mushroom soup, shredded cheddar and a can of chopped chilies, baked covered 20 minutes then uncovered 5-10 more and cut into thin wedges. One confirming search returned only chicken tortilla casseroles. Correctly notfound.

name: Toscakage -- Elva Adelsteinsdottir
flags: Titled with a personal attribution - Elva Adelsteinsdottir, an Icelandic name - so this is a handed-down card, not a published page. The dish itself is the Scandinavian toscakaka, a whipped-egg sponge finished with a cooked butter, sugar, cream and sliced-almond topping caramelized under a second bake, and there are many blog versions (True North Kitchen, The Sunday Baker, Baking with Butter, Nordic Kitchen Stories) - but none matches Elva's proportions and none is her recipe, so no link is recorded. Her version is also distinctive in being split into two layers and filled with macerated strawberries and whipped cream, which the published toscakakas do not do. GRAM NOTE: this card is already partly in grams (215 g sugar, 150 g flour) and the remaining conversions are 1 cube melted butter (8 Tbsp) = 113 g, topping 4 Tbsp butter = 57 g, 2 oz sliced almonds = 57 g, 2 oz sugar (4 Tbsp) = 50 g, 1 Tbsp flour = 8 g, 1-2 Tbsp heavy cream = 15-30 g.

name: Trifle
flags: Attributed to Jan Symmes. The card's voice and construction are unmistakably a 1990s women's-magazine lightened dessert - whipped cream cheese, 1 percent milk, 'light' frozen whipped topping, a decorating bag with a large star tube - so the ancestor is probably a Good Housekeeping or Woman's Day recipe of that period, but a search of the distinctive assembly (ladyfingers moistened with an orange juice and orange liqueur mixture, strawberries between, raspberries on top, 2 qt bowl, serves 16) turned up nothing matching. Not accepted; none of the published strawberry trifles found share this structure. Gram conversions: 8 oz whipped cream cheese = 227 g, 1/2 c 1% milk = 122 g, 1/4 c confectioners sugar = 30 g, 8 oz whipped topping = 227 g, 2 x 3 oz pkg ladyfingers = 170 g, 3/4 c orange juice = 180 g, 1/4 c orange liqueur = 57 g, 2 pints strawberries = about 600 g, 1/2 pint raspberries = about 170 g.

name: Vinaigrette
flags: House vinaigrette card, no source, and brand-specific in a way that points to personal notes rather than a publication - it names Pompeian red wine vinegar and Grey Poupon by name and gives both a kosher and a table salt measure. The ratio is a deliberate 3:1 oil to vinegar with the salt dissolved in the vinegar before the oil goes in, which is the standard technique; no published page matches these exact quantities. Correctly notfound. Gram conversions: 1/4 c red wine vinegar = 60 g, 1 1/2 tsp Dijon = 8 g, 1 1/4 tsp kosher salt (Diamond) = 4 g or 3/4 tsp table salt = 4.5 g, 3/4 c canola oil = 164 g.
